gist: A minister said a staggered age of consent will be discussed following the Russell Brand case.
Campaigner Mia Latter calls for making relationships between adults and 16 to 17-year-olds illegal.
Met Police are investigating separate sexual offence allegations against comedian David Walliams.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: Work and Pensions Secretary Pat McFadden confirmed that a staggered age of consent will be discussed. The proposal follows the conviction of comedian Russell Brand, who was jailed for 10-and-a-half years for rape and sexual assault. Campaigner Mia Latter, who alleged abuse by Brand when she was 16, wants relationships between adults and 16 to 17-year-olds criminalised while permitting teenage relationships.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: Under UK law, adults of any age can legally have sex with 16 and 17-year-olds. Campaign group Close the Consent Gap argues this creates a power imbalance, as people of this age are classified as children in other legal frameworks. Shadow Work and Pensions Secretary Helen Whately supported having a debate on changing the law.

sections.heading: What happens next
sections.text: Pat McFadden said he could not predict the conclusion of age of consent discussions. Meanwhile, Metropolitan Police are investigating comedian David Walliams over alleged serious sexual offences following reports by ITV News and the Guardian, which Walliams strongly denies.

gist: The US has lost its measles-free status after 26 years.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: The US has lost its measles elimination status after 26 years following uninterrupted transmission of the virus for over 12 months. Global health authorities announced the change as the country recorded more than 5,400 cases and up to 10 deaths in an ongoing outbreak.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: Experts say the resurgence is driven by persistent gaps in vaccination coverage and declining herd immunity. Some sources point to misinformation from officials including Robert F Kennedy Jr and Donald Trump, while others note a broader global trend and pandemic-era disruptions.

sections.heading: What happens next
sections.text: The US must submit corrective action plans and implement a national strategy to improve vaccination rates. Health officials are working to expand vaccine access, rebuild public trust, and regain elimination status.

gist: Cameron Bancroft claims the entire Australian team knew about the 2018 ball-tampering plot.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: Cameron Bancroft has published a detailed account claiming the entire Australian team and staff were aware of the 2018 sandpaper ball-tampering plot. He stated that he did not tell the full truth during the initial investigation to protect others. Bancroft specifically alleged that bowlers, including Pat Cummins, were involved in discussions about the ball's condition. He was prompted to speak out following a press conference by Cummins, which he described as making him feel betrayed.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: The revelations directly challenge the public denials issued by Pat Cummins and other Australian bowlers. This has reignited controversy surrounding the 2018 incident, placing significant pressure on the current captain ahead of upcoming Test matches. Cricket Australia faces renewed calls for transparency as the narrative shifts from individual blame to systemic team involvement.

sections.heading: What happens next
sections.text: Cricket Australia has established a forum to examine the events of 2018. It remains to be seen how those named by Bancroft will respond and whether the organisation will launch a more formal investigation into the claims.

gist: Offshore wind turbines are creating artificial reefs that attract various marine species.
Researchers are investigating whether these structures increase fish populations or merely concentrate them.
The transformation of the seafloor may significantly alter regional ecosystems and fishing practices.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: Offshore wind turbines installed off the US coast are functioning as artificial reefs. Structures attract algae and bivalves, subsequently drawing in fish like black sea bass. This phenomenon, observed at the Block Island windfarm, mirrors effects seen at shipwrecks and European wind projects.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: Scientists are debating whether turbines increase total fish production or simply aggregate existing populations. This shift could change the composition of marine life, potentially favouring reef-oriented species over those preferring open spaces. It also impacts commercial fishing, as fish clustering near turbines may affect traditional mobile gear usage.

sections.heading: What happens next
sections.text: Researchers are conducting long-term studies to understand the ecological consequences of these artificial reefs. Ongoing work involves monitoring fish behaviour and collaborating with commercial fishers to adapt to the changing environment. Future data will clarify if these projects ultimately benefit or harm the fishing industry.

sections.text: The Bureau of Statistics reported a 1.0% rise in private sector wages for the September quarter. sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: A Spanish national court launched an investigation into singer Julio Iglesias following complaints from two former female staff members. The women, who worked for him in the Bahamas and the Dominican Republic, allege he subjected them to sexual abuse, physical assault and degrading treatment in 2021. Prosecutors previously dropped an inquiry due to jurisdiction issues, but a judge has now opened criminal proceedings based on preliminary evidence, including photographs of injuries.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: The case highlights the legal scope for Spanish courts to prosecute crimes committed abroad by Spanish citizens. Iglesias, a renowned Latin music artist, has consistently denied all accusations, calling them false.

sections.heading: What happens next
sections.text: The investigating judge has summoned the two former employees to testify in person on 3 February. The court will examine charges relating to sexual freedom, assault and degrading treatment.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: Alice Webb paid Jordan Parke £2,300 for a non-surgical Brazilian Butt Lift in September 2024. Parke injected 1,400ml of filler. Webb collapsed at a house in Gloucester and died in hospital the next day.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: A pathologist found filler blocked blood vessels in Webb's vital organs. Parke lacked medical training and had previous bans from performing BBLs.

sections.text: The inquest into Webb's death continues. Criminal proceedings against Parke could not proceed because he died earlier this year.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: Birmingham City Council secured an interim High Court injunction preventing unauthorised flags from being attached to lamp-posts and highway infrastructure. Thousands of union jacks and St George's flags had been put up by supporters of the campaign group Raise the Colours. Judge Emma Kelly granted the order, applying to group leader Ryan Bridge and others, citing safety risks and a compelling need.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: The council argued the displays created danger, obstruction, and fueled community tensions, noting incidents of intimidation and a broken leg. Campaigners opposed the move, arguing it infringed upon freedom of expression and political protest rights under the European Convention on Human Rights.

sections.heading: What happens next
sections.text: The interim injunction remains in place until a trial or further court order. A further hearing in the case was scheduled to take place on Thursday.

fivew: Birmingham City Council, Judge Emma Kelly, and Raise the Colours leader Ryan Bridge.

The council sought the order due to safety risks, obstruction, and tensions caused by unauthorised flag displays.

quotes.text: For me, the union flag represents home, identity, belonging, national identity, British culture and patriotism.

Changes are driven by age and fertility differences rather than religious conversion.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: A new Pew Research Center study projects global religious populations to 2070. It estimates India will remain overwhelmingly Hindu, shifting from 79% in 2020 to 76% by 2070. Meanwhile, the Muslim share is projected to rise from 15% to 20%.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: The shift is driven largely by younger median ages and higher fertility rates among Indian Muslims compared to Hindus. Demographers note that alarmist narratives regarding conversion are unfounded, as current trends show the fertility gap is narrowing.

sections.heading: What happens next
sections.text: India will remain the world's second-largest Muslim population by 2070, behind Pakistan. Hindu populations in India are still expected to grow by 176 million over the period.

fivew: A Pew Research Center study projected India's religious makeup up to 2070.

timeline.text: ‘It’s a biohazard’: Native communities in US south-west try to recover after flooding intensified by El Niño

gist: Native communities in the US south-west are recovering from severe El Niño-driven floods.
The San Juan River reached historic levels, damaging wastewater facilities and contaminating crops.
Displaced residents face significant challenges, including insurance gaps and property losses.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: Unprecedented rain intensified by El Niño caused once-in-a-generation flooding in the Four Corners region. The San Juan River crested at 21ft near Shiprock, causing wastewater treatment facilities to fail and sewage to enter the river. Residents were ordered to evacuate, and homes, farms and roads were submerged.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: The floods created severe biohazards with high levels of E coli and treatment chemicals in soil and water. Farmers lost entire crops and face heavy financial losses, while tribal trust land issues complicate crop insurance. Displaced families struggle with power outages and lack clear support.

sections.heading: What happens next
sections.text: Evacuees in temporary housing must secure funds for deposits to extend their stay. Communities and local groups continue providing food, supplies and animal shelter while residents await safe road conditions to begin rebuilding.

fivew: Navajo and other native residents, farmers, and local community organizers.
Native communities experienced severe once-in-a-generation flooding.
The Four Corners region of the south-west US, including Shiprock.
Heavy thunderstorms and rains were intensified by El Niño.

sections.text: The Danish parliament voted unanimously to approve a security pact involving Denmark, Greenland and the US. This agreement updates a 1951 defence treaty, granting the US underwater access and permission to build missile defence infrastructure. The deal follows months of negotiations and has already received approval from the Greenlandic parliament.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: The treaty aims to improve relations following tensions caused by previous threats regarding the territory. It formally recognises Greenland as an equal partner and provides a framework for future cooperation. Furthermore, it guarantees that Greenland would remain part of Nato if it achieves full independence from Denmark.

sections.heading: What happens next
sections.text: The agreement requires a final notification from the US president to the US Congress to become effective. While the framework is now established, Danish officials noted that rebuilding trust remains a significant task. There are currently no confirmed plans from the US regarding the establishment of new military bases.

gist: Prosecutors knew an expert witness in Lucy Letby's trial was under investigation.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: Prof Peter Hindmarsh gave expert medical evidence during the trial of Lucy Letby. While the trial was ongoing, his employer barred him from clinical practice and referred him to the General Medical Council over safety concerns. The jury and the defence were not told of these developments or of a subsequent tribunal ruling.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: Hindmarsh provided crucial testimony suggesting babies were poisoned with insulin. Legal experts state that failing to disclose material information about an expert witness's credibility or disciplinary proceedings could be grounds for an appeal and raises questions about the safety of convictions.

sections.heading: What happens next
sections.text: Letby's lawyer has applied to the Criminal Cases Review Commission for her convictions to be referred back to the court of appeal. Meanwhile, questions remain over what the police and prosecution knew and when.

fivew: Lucy Letby's lawyer called for an urgent review of her convictions after revelations about an expert witness.
Crucial safety concerns and disciplinary investigations regarding a key medical expert witness were not disclosed at trial.

quotes.text: These revelations about Prof Hindmarsh, and the failure to disclose material information about him to the defence at trial, raise fundamental questions

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: The International Court of Justice ruled that genocide was committed against the Rohingya people in Myanmar. The court inferred genocidal intent from the actions of Myanmar's security forces and local militias.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: The judgement clarifies the evidentiary standard required to prove genocide. This decision has implications for other cases, including South Africa's case against Israel regarding Gaza. The UK called for UN Security Council action and expelled Myanmar's defence attache in London.

sections.heading: What happens next
sections.text: The ICJ ordered Myanmar to make reparations to the Rohingya people. However, the court lacks enforcement mechanisms, and the Myanmar government is unlikely to accept the ruling quietly. Any UN Security Council resolution could face a veto from China or Russia.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: Outgoing Republican senator John Cornyn blocked Donald Trump's nomination of T Elliot Gaiser for a district court in northern Texas. This followed a heated verbal argument on the Senate floor between Cornyn and fellow Texas Republican senator Ted Cruz regarding the nomination. Cornyn withheld his blue slip, preventing the Senate judiciary committee from moving Gaiser forward.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: The block disrupts Republican plans to approve Trump's judicial nominations before Congress recesses and Democrats take control of Congress in January. Cruz stated that leaving the seat vacant would give it to the Democrats. The justice department criticized Cornyn for choosing political obstruction, while the Heritage Foundation president also condemned the decision.

timeline.text: More climate money for Africa? Europe says use what's already pledged

gist: African negotiators at COP31 requested a tripling of climate adaptation finance by 2035.
The European Union argued that existing pledged funds must be delivered before setting new targets.
Twenty-three African nations have not yet submitted required National Adaptation Plans to the UN.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: At the COP31 UN climate summit in Turkey, the African Group of Negotiators pushed to triple adaptation finance by 2035. The proposal was not accepted for formal negotiations. European Union officials stated that the focus should be on deploying already pledged climate funds rather than establishing new targets. Meanwhile, 23 African countries have not submitted National Adaptation Plans to the UN.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: Sub-Saharan Africa requires around $51bn annually for adaptation, but developing nations received only about 10% of needed global funds in 2024. Without National Adaptation Plans, securing climate financing is more difficult for vulnerable nations suffering from severe droughts and floods. However, experts note that lack of support and technical capacity prevents these countries from preparing the required plans.

sections.heading: What happens next
sections.text: African negotiators continue to push for increased funding commitments. The European Union called for improvements in helping developing countries access existing climate funds that remain undeployed.

sections.text: Gita Navekar waited two years for a diagnosis before a private scan revealed rare pelvic cancer. She lived for 11 years before passing away in April 2021. sections.text: The United States held its first deep-sea mining lease auction off American Samoa, selling two seabed tracts to sole bidder Wetstone US Ventures for $3m each. The auction proceeded despite a federal judge in Hawaii voiding the project's environmental clearance under the Endangered Species Act.

Friday night will be ‘coldest of the autumn so far’, UK forecasters say

gist: The UK is expected to experience its coldest night of autumn so far.
Temperatures could fall to minus 10C in rural Scotland overnight on Friday.
Cold weather health alerts are active alongside 12 flood alerts across England.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: Thursday night brought temperatures down to minus 8.4C at Tulloch Bridge in the Scottish Highlands, making it the coldest night of autumn until Friday. Cold Arctic air has moved southwards across the UK, bringing frost, rain, and wintry showers to northern areas while southern regions remained milder.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: The UK Health Security Agency issued yellow cold health alerts for parts of northern England until Monday morning due to potential impacts on healthcare services and vulnerable people. Additionally, 12 flood alerts are active in England. The colder autumn weather also boosted supermarket clothing sales volume by 1.5 per cent, helping overall retail sales recover unexpectedly.

sections.heading: What happens next
sections.text: Friday night is forecast to become the coldest of autumn so far, with temperatures potentially reaching minus 10C in rural Scotland. Widespread frost will develop across the Midlands, northern England, Northern Ireland and Scotland. Saturday is expected to be mostly dry with sunshine.

gist: Retail sales rose by 0.7% in October following the government Be Ready campaign launch.
Households stockpiled long-life food and essentials like tinned goods and UHT milk.
Fuel sales fell due to rising prices, while clothing and gallery visits increased.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: British retail sales surged by 0.7% in October as the public responded to the government's Be Ready emergency preparedness campaign by buying long-life food, tinned goods, and UHT milk. Clothing, footwear, and gallery visits also increased, though motor fuel sales fell by 2.2%.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: The stockpile surge defied economists' predictions of flat or falling sales, providing a welcome bounce back for the retail industry after a poor September. However, analysts suggest households only need to stock cupboards once, which could lead to slower food sales growth ahead.

gist: A truck killed three people at a Tsawwassen First Nation ceremony near Vancouver.

Community members are gathering their own evidence due to a lack of answers.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: A black pickup truck towing an equipment trailer breached a curb outside a mall near Vancouver, striking a group gathered for a Tsawwassen First Nation ceremony. Virginia Splockton and wilapiya were killed at the scene, and Gwenyth Brigid Dwyn died later in hospital. Minutes earlier, the same truck had struck another vehicle nearby. Police released the driver from the hospital the same day without charges, suggesting a preliminary medical emergency.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: Families and community members are outraged by the lack of arrests and communication from Delta police. They argue officers rushed to conclusions about a medical emergency, leaving grieving families to gather their own evidence and video footage.

sections.heading: What happens next
sections.text: Police stated they are still investigating the movements of the vehicle and the possibility of a medical event, adding that charges would be laid if evidence establishes criminality.

gist: A new study reveals most US prisoners were victims of violent crime before incarceration.
Experts argue that bolstering trauma recovery resources can help break the cycle of crime.
Jemaine Hunter shares his experience of childhood trauma and decades in prison.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: A new study by Just Safe found that 84% of people in US prisons or jails were victims of violent crime before their first incarceration. The nationally representative survey of 20,000 Americans showed that half experienced caregiver abuse and one-third faced sexual or intimate partner violence.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: Experts say the findings show the need to reframe crime politics by focusing on trauma recovery rather than punishment alone. Unaddressed pain can lead individuals to turn to drugs, alcohol, or further violence, trapping them in the justice system.

stories.title: TfL photocard breach exposes 265,000 customers
stories.standfirst: Names, addresses, dates of birth and security answers were accessed, Transport for London says.

articles.title: TfL photocard breach exposes 265,000 customers
articles.standfirst: Names, addresses, dates of birth and security answers were accessed, Transport for London says.

timeline.text: TfL photocard breach exposes 265,000 customers

gist: Transport for London experienced a cyber breach affecting Oyster photocard customers.
Personal details were accessed, but financial information remained secure.
The photocard website was taken offline for investigation.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: Transport for London detected suspicious activity on its photocard website, leading to a cyber breach that compromised personal data of approximately 265,000 customers. Names, addresses, contact details, dates of birth and security questions were accessed. Transport for London took the website offline to limit access and reported the incident to the Information Commissioner's Office. Financial details and journey history were not compromised.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: This incident exposes personal details for a large number of customers and marks the second time in just over two years that the system has faced a cyber disruption, following a previous attack in September 2024.

sections.heading: What happens next
sections.text: The photocard website remains offline while investigations continue. Customers are currently unable to apply for or renew photocards online, though they can continue to travel and may contact customer services for assistance.

fivew: Personal details of Oyster photocard customers were accessed in a cyber breach.
Suspicious activity was detected on the photocard website.

gist: The FA explored challenging Gianni Infantino running for a fourth Fifa term.
The FA decided a legal challenge would likely fail against the Fifa council decision.
Fair Square urged the FA to pursue action through Fifa governance.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: The Football Association looked into challenging Gianni Infantino standing for another term as Fifa leader. Fair Square contacted the FA arguing that the ruling on term limits could face legal action and urged the FA to request his disqualification. FA chair Debbie Hewitt replied that the governing body examined the possibility but concluded a challenge would not succeed.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: Fifa rules normally restrict leaders to three terms, but the council decided Infantino's initial partial period did not count towards this limit. Fair Square stated that abandoning challenge channels tells the leader he can act without consequence.

sections.heading: What happens next
sections.text: Fair Square intends to encourage the FA to keep its options open regarding the matter. An election is scheduled for March.

fivew: The Football Association and Fair Square.

Ahead of the election in March.
Fair Square argued that discounting his first partial period violated Fifa statutes.

gist: Leon Smith is stepping down as Great Britain Davis Cup captain after seventeen years.
He guided the team to a historic title victory in 2015.
His final tournament in charge will be the upcoming Finals in Bologna.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: Great Britain Davis Cup captain Leon Smith announced he is leaving his post after nearly seventeen years. He will step down following the upcoming Finals in Bologna. The Lawn Tennis Association has spoken to potential candidates but has not yet named a successor.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: Smith took charge in 2010 when the team faced relegation. He successfully revived the squad and led them to their first title since 1936 in the year 2015, supported by player Andy Murray.

sections.heading: What happens next
sections.text: Smith hopes to achieve another successful run at the Bologna Finals. Afterwards, he will remain in his position as the head of British men's tennis while the LTA searches for his replacement.

timeline.text: F1 to introduce full-time race stewards from 2027

gist: Formula 1 will introduce permanent race stewards from the 2027 season.
The change addresses driver criticisms regarding inconsistent penalty decisions for on-track incidents.
Driver stewards and existing FIA stewards will continue to play a vital role.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: The FIA announced it will introduce permanent race stewards starting in 2027 following consistent calls from grand prix drivers. A small number of full-time stewards will be recruited during 2027, with the group expanding from 2028.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: Drivers have frequently complained that penalty rulings were applied inconsistently. The FIA stated that dedicated full-time stewards will provide continuity, expertise, and greater consistency in decision-making.

sections.heading: What happens next
sections.text: The FIA will begin recruiting permanent stewards for a phased introduction during the 2027 season, while continuing to use driver stewards and existing personnel on a mixed roster.

fivew: To provide continuity and expertise and improve consistency in decision-making.

quotes.text: F1 and the FIA all agree that permanent stewards should be the way forward
This latest major investment in FIA officiating reflects our dedication to delivering the highest standards of decision-making, fairness and integrity in motorsport.

stories.title: Shevchenko accuses Mudryk camp of 'baseless slander'
stories.standfirst: Ukraine great Andriy Shevchenko accuses Mykhailo Mudryk of a "baseless slander" after the on-loan Tottenham winger blamed his failed drugs test on the nation's football association.

articles.title: Shevchenko accuses Mudryk camp of 'baseless slander'
articles.standfirst: Ukraine great Andriy Shevchenko accuses Mykhailo Mudryk of a "baseless slander" after the on-loan Tottenham winger blamed his failed drugs test on the nation's football association.

timeline.text: Shevchenko accuses Mudryk camp of 'baseless slander'

gist: Andriy Shevchenko accused Mykhailo Mudryk's camp of seeking a false scapegoat for a doping test.
Mudryk blamed the Ukrainian Association of Football for his failed test and subsequent 20-month ban.
Shevchenko denied the allegations, defending the association and asking Mudryk to retract his comments.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: Andriy Shevchenko stated that Mykhailo Mudryk's representatives repeatedly asked for a football federation employee to falsely take the blame for Mudryk's positive test for meldonium. Mudryk, suspended from November 2024 to July 2026, blamed the Ukrainian Association of Football for the failed test, claiming it happened on international duty and criticizing a lack of support.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: Shevchenko called the claims baseless slander and defended the professionalism of association staff, while Mudryk argued the handling of the matter delayed his return to football.

fivew: Andriy Shevchenko accused Mykhailo Mudryk's representatives of asking an employee to falsely take the blame for a positive drugs test.
Mudryk blamed the Ukrainian Association of Football for his failed drugs test, prompting a public response from Shevchenko.

quotes.text: baseless slander against our people, who do their work honestly and professionally
Head coach Serhiy Rebrov also approved for Mykhailo to have two of his personal specialists work with him at the training camps
